Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

Today, we're going to see the clippers.

Key details

  • Clippers are those circuits which are made up of electronic components such as diodes, resistors, and DC bias voltages, which are used to remove a part of the waveform without disturbing the other part of the waveform.
  • That means to say, in case you have a square waveform, as shown in the figure here.
  • If I need only the positive part of the waveform and I don't want the negative part, using the clipper circuit, we can get only the positive part.
  • Further, the series clipper can be grouped into unbiased series clipper, biased series clipper, and in parallel, it's been classified into unbiased parallel and biased parallel.
  • The series configuration is defined as one where diode is in series with the load.
  • Figure 1A, we are using a series unbiased clipper.
  • First of all, what is this unbiased?
  • Unbiased means there is no DC supply used in the circuit.
  • Only we have in this block, we have only diode and the resistor.
  • In case if there is any bias voltage here along with the resistor or along with the diode, other than the supply voltage.
  • Other than the supply voltage, if we have a voltages here, a DC voltage, then it is biased.
  • If the diode is connected in series with the resistor, it is called as a series configuration.
  • The response of the series configuration of Figure 1 to the variety of alternating waveform is as shown in the figure B.
  • That means to say, variety of the input is first, in the diagram here, which I'm pointing, it is a square waveform.
  • The output of the series clipper will be only the positive off cycle, negative has been clipped off.
  • Similarly, we have next, in the place of square, we have a triangle waveform.
  • That means we need to understand that there's no boundary, where we can also use a sine waveform, the sawtooth waveform, et cetera, as an input signal and based on the circuit, like a clipper, the output variations can be obtained.
  • Figure shows here.
  • Figure shows a series clipper with a DC bias supply.
  • This is what I was referring previously.
  • When there is a DC bias here, it is called as a series clipper with a bias or a series clipper with a DC supply.
  • This configuration is called as a biased series clipper.
  • The addition of a DC supply to the network as shown in the figure can have a pronounced effect on an analysis of a series clipper configuration.
  • That means there could be some change in the output of which the DC supply can be in the leg between the supply and the output or in a branch parallel to the output.
  • It can be at any place.
  • One, it can be between the input and the diode, or diode and the resistor, or resistor and the output.
  • It can be anywhere.
  • The output response is not as obvious because the DC can aid or work as a source voltage.
  • That means the DC source, which is there here, can aid in the sense it can have an addition with the voltage applied here or it can subtract with the voltage applied here.
  • That we will understand with the analysis in the next slide.
  • The step one as shown here, take careful note of where the output voltage to be defined.

Core explanation · 10:00–14:59

Now let us solve a numerical example one.

Key details

  • The question is, determine the output waveform for a sinusoidal input of figure seven.
  • This is figure seven.
  • I have a sinusoidal signal here.
  • VI 20 volts is a peak to peak of one cycle.
  • Step two, the positive region of the VI and the DC are both working in the same direction to turn on.
  • So the applied total voltage is 10 plus 5 because both are in the same direction.
  • We have plus is there, and we have plus is there, it get added.
  • The result is that we can safely assume the diode is in on state for entire region of positive cycle voltage.
  • Once the supply goes negative, it will have exceeded the.
  • DC supply voltage of 5, therefore it would turn off.
  • What is the transition model?
  • If VI and the DC voltage is greater than the diode cutting voltage, that is VD is equal to zero, then the diode is in on condition.
  • Diode is on.
  • Therefore, we apply the KVL over there.
  • If you apply the KVL over there, VI plus 5 is equal to zero, so VI is equal to minus 5 volts we get.
  • Minus 5 volts.
  • For a voltage less than 5, the diode is in open circuit and the output is zero, as shown in the sketch of the VOUT.
  • This is what we want to prove here.
  • Using the figure number nine, we find that for a condition when a diode is on and the diode current is established, the output voltage will be following.
  • So the analysis of the clipper circuit with the square wave input is actually easier than the sinusoidal because only two levels are to be considered.
  • The transition is important.
  • It is clipped off.
  • For a transition from 0 to T/2, the figure 11.
  • Result, the diode is in short circuit state, that is on.
  • If we apply the KVL, we get VOUT is equal to 20 plus 20, 25 volts is the applied voltage.
  • Then for VI is equal to -10 during the negative cycle, diode is off.
  • That is VOUT is equal to zero.
  • Unless we get a positive cycle only, and during the negative cycle, we won't see the output waveform.
  • It is clipped off.

Example or application from the lecture

  • Then coming to the circuit here, we have a biased clipper here, series biased clipper, where resistor is connected in series with the diode and voltage 5 volts is given, and VI is equal to 20.
  • That means to say in the place of sine, if you have a square, only two places if you consider it is more than, whereas here we need to consider for all the places here.
  • So this is the solution for example number one, where we see that during the positive cycle, diode is on, during the negative cycle it is off.
